title: AI Leaders Are Refineries, Not Native-App Winners
dek: AI enters the agent era: first-phase leaders are just refineries, not native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations must shift from jobs to tasks; ultimately, humans compete on creativity that creates something from nothing.
why: Zeng Ming offers a three-stage industrial history framework to give you a coordinate system for locating AI's current position—a cure for the optimism of 'this time is different'—while also revealing the window of opportunity for application entrepreneurs and the brutal expectations for giants in transition.
who: CEOs making AI strategy, executives at traditional giants seeking a second curve, AI investors, and tech founders torn between building models or applications.
skip: The rapid-fire Q&A and book list at the end can be skipped (after 2:29).

points.h: Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
points.body: Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of general-purpose technologies into three stages: first becoming social infrastructure, then an explosion of applications, and finally the emergence of native applications. The consensus forming around tokens as a unit of measurement by 2026 signals the maturity of the first stage; the agent events around the Spring Festival (colloquially called 'lobster') mark AI's official entry into the agent era. He draws an analogy to the website-building movement of 1992: back then people built websites to share information; today they build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet; those who can establish agent standards and capture user entry points may hold the biggest opportunity of the next two years.

points.h: A ten-trillion-dollar company will emerge, but not these two
points.body: Zeng Ming states plainly that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technical and commercial achievements, but business history shows that the first wave of companies to break out are likely not the big winners of the native-application stage. Yahoo reached a $120 billion market cap five years after founding, and AOL's valuation hit $220 billion, yet neither became the Google of its era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies—refineries that extract base oil—while the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies, and cars were not built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will certainly emerge, but it may not be one of the current leaders. Model companies will evolve into a mature business of oligopoly plus heavy government regulation.

points.h: The unit of AI-native organizations is tasks, not jobs
points.body: Corporations correspond to the hierarchical system of the industrial age; AI disrupts the industrial age, and the corporate system will decline. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not a job but a task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow around 'what problem needs solving,' with humans and AI collaborating around tasks. Thus, well-designed positions and hierarchies will disappear, and traditional middle management will also die out. Future founders must first define their organization's task network. Silicon Valley's New Lab is a prototype of the new organizational form; OpenAI itself resembles a lab more than a traditional company. The culture of new organizations is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing, and co-creation, rather than command and assessment.

points.h: Excellence is judged only in hindsight; being good is visible on the spot
points.body: Zeng Ming argues that 'excellent is not the same as great.' Excellence is growth sustained by positive feedback, while greatness requires overcoming repeated negative feedback, persisting when everyone disapproves, and ultimately proving oneself a prophet of the era through enormous success—so 'greatness is determined after the fact.' Those who are merely excellent easily fall into a cycle of proving themselves, leading to conservative strategies. Truly great people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the era and their partners, and are driven by mission rather than external valuation. When identifying founders, he asks, 'What kind of self would you be satisfied with in ten years?' If the answer is 'a company worth ten billion dollars,' that is mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly great founders are often altruistic and empathetic.

points.h: Strategy in the AI era cannot be planned; it must be generated
points.body: In the AI era, strategy is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a 'strategy generation system': organizations must build an environment and network that allows strategic insights to emerge naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality demands are greater, CEOs cannot rely on linear extrapolation for planning, nor can they outsource strategy to McKinsey—McKinsey's rise was a product of the slow maturation of the industrial era. His methodology is 'look ten years, think three years, act one year,' with the core being 'think three years': you need to see at least two or three milestones ahead, creating tension between short-term actions and the medium-term vision. Organizational building must ensure sufficient context rather than control, enabling the right people to make the right decisions at the right time.

points.h: The right analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
points.body: Zeng Ming believes robots are still in the strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. Two current paths—building a generalized brain first or closing the loop in specific scenarios first—are both logically valid, and it's impossible to know in advance which will be faster. Historically, the automobile industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and it wasn't until Ford built the assembly line in 1913 that scaling began; robots haven't yet had their Model T moment, and whoever truly sells ten thousand robots first would already be remarkable. But a better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented, refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, and countless other categories emerged. Robots interacting with the physical world will have N major scenarios, and home, companionship, and industrial uses may each produce their own native giants.

points.h: Giants that feel safe are the least safe
points.body: Zeng Ming says that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe; feeling safe is the most unsafe of all. In business history, no company from one era has smoothly transitioned to the next; IBM and Microsoft are the only two possible exceptions, and both are fraught with uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that disrupts the industrial revolution, not a continuation innovation like mobile internet, so the technological reserves and organizational culture of old giants are liabilities. Google can survive as an AI cloud company, but it may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is not naturally safe either. New platforms will most likely be created by new companies.

points.h: Human value lies in creating from nothing, not in writing songs or painting
points.body: Borrowing Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the age of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI. Humans are both forced and finally liberated to develop new potential. This potential is creativity—not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and create something from nothing. AI has already taken all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. Hence he calls his mission 'to be a happy researcher' and believes civilization's next step will reorganize around creativity, even forcing the education system to shift from 'knowledge indoctrination' to 'open exploration,' because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

terms.def: Treating AI compute as infrastructure that produces tokens, symbolizing intelligence entering a standardized pricing stage.
An operating system that can directly dispatch all agents to complete tasks based on intent; Zeng Ming believes it belongs to the third stage and cannot be implemented yet.
A new organizational form dissatisfied with the corporate system, centered on researchers; OpenAI is seen as the earliest example.
A Silicon Valley buzzword meaning taking control of one's own destiny, proactively seeking tasks and growth, replacing hierarchical command.
A management philosophy: provide ample shared context and information so members can autonomously make correct decisions.

quotes.text: The most successful companies must be contrarian, but being contrarian does not guarantee success.
It may not survive to the end. It will likely do well later on, but it is probably not the big player, the big winner of the native application stage.
Companies in the first stage find it hard to survive into the second stage, and companies in the second stage find it hard to survive into the third stage.

So companies will disappear; companies will die out. There's nothing to regret about that. In the future there will be more fun things—how many people actually enjoy going to work at a company now? They don't.

My technology is so great, I've created so much value, why might my company not be worth much? Because of the basic laws of economics: as long as there is homogeneous supply, you cannot capture high profits—you are just a company that isn't worth much.

Greatness is determined after the fact, because you overcome negative feedback again and again, and when everyone disapproves of you, you ultimately prove through enormous success that you were the earliest prophet of the era.
I have always believed that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe; whoever feels safe is the most unsafe.
